messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Michael, an African-American UX Designer at a tech startup in San Francisco, has been grappling with profound anxiety since a traumatic stalking incident last year. At nineteen, he felt like his world had turned upside down when a former acquaintance began following him relentlessly, leaving ominous messages and making unwanted contact late into the night. The intensity of this harassment led to a moment where Michael was cornered in an alley near his apartment building by the stalker, who threatened him physically before being chased away by a passerby. This experience has left Michael with a deep sense that the world is dangerous. He constantly feels on edge and believes that he must maintain constant vigilance to protect himself from any potential threats. "The world is a dangerous place," he often thinks, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios as he walks home late at night or even during daylight hours in less populated areas. Michael has come to believe that the stalking happened because of how he acted. He feels an overwhelming sense of self-blame, thinking about all the decisions and actions he took that may have triggered this unwanted attention. "Maybe if I had just avoided him from the start," he often reflects, feeling a deep regret and remorse for not having been more cautious earlier. His occupation as a UX Designer has made it particularly challenging to navigate his fears. He avoids working late at the office, fearing that staying past normal hours would leave him vulnerable to another encounter with his stalker. This avoidance behavior has led to strained relationships with colleagues who expect evening check-ins and collaborative sessions. Michael’s performance at work is affected by his need for constant vigilance; he often finds himself distracted during meetings or design reviews, always scanning the environment for potential threats. Michael’s self-imposed isolation extends beyond work into his personal life. He avoids social gatherings and public spaces where the risk of encountering someone who might threaten him seems high. This has made it difficult to maintain any meaningful connections outside of a small circle of close friends who understand his fears but sometimes feel helpless in their ability to support him fully. What frightens Michael most is the fear that this feeling of constant danger will never abate. He worries that he will always be looking over his shoulder, unable to relax or enjoy life without anxiety gripping him. It was a particularly harrowing night last week when Michael felt like he couldn’t take it anymore. His stalker had sent a threatening message on social media late at night, and Michael found himself trapped in bed, unable to sleep due to the overwhelming sense of dread. It is this fear that finally brought Michael to seek help. He hopes to regain some semblance of normalcy and find ways to navigate his world without constant vigilance weighing him down. What he most hopes for is to be able to trust others again, to engage with life on a deeper level, and to live without the ever-present specter of danger looming over every decision and action. Michael’s journey toward healing is one that requires addressing these deep-seated beliefs about his world being dangerous and finding ways to challenge the self-blame that has taken root. Through therapy, he aims to learn coping strategies that can help him manage his anxiety without avoiding everything that reminds him of the past trauma.
